summary: Describes the data transport protocols used by WebRTC, the browser technology for real-time audio, video and data. It covers how traffic travels between peers and how it interacts with middleboxes such as firewalls, relays and NAT boxes. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Two friends far apart want to video chat. This document explains the roads and rules their browsers use to send sound, pictures and messages, even when gates and guards in between try to block the way.

subtitle: The transport rules every WebRTC endpoint must follow to get media and data through NATs, firewalls and relays.

tldr.problem: WebRTC peers sit behind NAT boxes, firewalls and other middleboxes, and need agreed transports so that interactive media and data can still flow.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requires full ICE, TURN (including over TCP and TLS), ICE-TCP, DTLS-SRTP key exchange and SCTP over DTLS for data channels, and sets rules for IPv6 address use, send prioritization and DSCP marking.
tldr.outcome: Conforming endpoints have a common baseline for connectivity, bundling and prioritization, and security considerations are delegated to other WebRTC documents.

today: RFC 8835 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021 and, per the metadata for this unit, has not been obsoleted or updated. It sits alongside RFC 8831 and RFC 8832 for data channels.

sections.title: Scope of the Transport Rules
sections.content:
WebRTC is a protocol suite for real-time multimedia exchange between browsers, and between browsers and other entities. This document focuses on the data transport protocols conforming implementations use, including how they interact with intermediate boxes such as firewalls, relays and NAT boxes.

It uses terminology from the WebRTC overview, RFC 8825, and the requirements apply to all WebRTC endpoints unless a requirement is called out as applying only to WebRTC browsers. The suite is intended to satisfy the security considerations in RFC 8826 and RFC 8827.
sections.eli5: This is the rulebook for how a browser's calls travel across the internet past gates and guards.

sections.title: System-Provided Interfaces and IP Versions
sections.content:
The protocols assume the platform provides UDP (RFC 768), which most protocol elements use, and TCP (RFC 793), used for HTTP/WebSockets, TURN/TLS and ICE-TCP. For UDP, the specification assumes the ability to set the DSCP per packet, though it does not assume the markings will be honored, since they may be zeroed or changed. It does not assume access to ICMP or raw IP, and platforms lacking these interfaces cannot support a conforming endpoint.

Applications in a WebRTC browser MUST be able to use both IPv4 and IPv6 where available, so two peers with only one IP version in common can still communicate. The "Happy Eyeballs" specification for ICE (RFC 8421) SHOULD be supported.
sections.eli5: A browser has to be able to speak on both the old and the new kind of internet address, and use the basic delivery services the computer gives it.

sections.title: Temporary IPv6 Addresses
sections.content:
Normal IPv6 address selection prefers privacy-enhancing temporary addresses over permanent ones. In ICE that rule does not have the right effect, because all addresses are gathered and revealed to the application. So the RFC applies a different rule: when both nondeprecated temporary and permanent addresses of the same scope are present, the endpoint SHOULD discard the permanent ones before exposing addresses to the application or using them in ICE.

If only some temporary addresses are deprecated, the endpoint SHOULD discard the deprecated ones unless an ongoing connection uses them. During an ICE restart, deprecated addresses currently in use MAY be retained.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are like a throwaway nickname and some are your real name. The browser hides the real name and only shows the nickname.

sections.title: Getting Through Middleboxes
sections.content:
The primary mechanism is ICE, which handles NATs and simple stateful firewalls that let traffic in only in response to outbound traffic. Endpoints MUST implement full ICE, not ICE-Lite. Where both parties are behind NATs doing endpoint-dependent mapping, TURN MUST be supported, and browsers MUST support configuring STUN and TURN servers from both browser configuration and an application.

For firewalls that block all UDP, TURN over TCP and TURN over TLS over TCP MUST both be supported. TURN extensions for IPv6 MUST be supported, and ICE-TCP candidates MUST be supported, which can let peers with public addresses connect across UDP-blocking firewalls without a TURN server. Where TCP is used, RTP framing from RFC 4571 MUST be used for all packets, including RTP, DTLS and STUN connectivity checks.

TURN TCP candidates (RFC 6062) MAY be supported but are seen as offering little benefit, partly because TCP between the TURN server and the peer may cause head-of-line blocking. The ALTERNATE-SERVER mechanism (300 Try Alternate) MUST be supported. HTTP proxy access is optional; if used, the ALPN header and proxy authentication MUST be supported.
sections.eli5: If a direct road is blocked, the browser tries other roads, and as a last resort asks a helper in the middle to pass messages along.

sections.title: Transport Protocols for Media and Data
sections.content:
Media uses secure RTP, with details in RFC 8834, which mandates a circuit breaker and congestion control. Key exchange MUST use DTLS-SRTP as described in RFC 8827.

For data channels, endpoints MUST support SCTP over DTLS over ICE, as specified in RFC 8261, with SDP negotiation in RFC 8841. The SCTP I-DATA extension (RFC 8260) MUST be supported, as must the channel setup protocol in RFC 8832. Because all ICE candidate pairs for a component belong to the same DTLS association, there is only one DTLS handshake even with several valid pairs.

Endpoints MUST support multiplexing DTLS and RTP over the same port pair, and all application-layer payloads over the DTLS connection are SCTP packets. Protocol identification MUST be supplied in the DTLS handshake, as specified in RFC 8833.
sections.eli5: Calls use a locked, secure kind of audio-and-video delivery, and chat-like messages ride in a separate locked tunnel on the same road.

sections.title: Prioritizing Media and Data
sections.content:
The application sets a priority for each media flow or data flow (the outgoing data on one data channel). The API has four levels: very-low, low, medium and high. Priority affects both packet send order and packet markings.

For local prioritization, when several streams share one congestion control regime, the endpoint SHOULD give each stream at each level approximately twice the transmission capacity (in payload bytes) of the level below. So a high-priority flow can send 8 times as much as a very-low one when both have data. The RFC's example: a high-priority audio flow with 100-byte packets and a low-priority video flow with 1000-byte packets would, given room for more than 5000 payload bytes, send 4000 bytes of audio and 1000 bytes of video.

Implementations may configure per-codec and per-channel target rates, or use weighted round-robin. For media, deep queues are usually inappropriate; for reliable data, queues are useful.
sections.eli5: When the road is jammed, important traffic gets a bigger share. Each step up in importance gets about double the space of the step below.

sections.title: DSCP Marking and Bundling
sections.content:
Implementations SHOULD attempt to set DSCP markings according to RFC 8837, but MAY turn them off if they detect problems such as priority inversion or blocked packets. One suggested way to detect blocked markings is to send initial ICE probes with DSCP 0 and then probe each DSCP intended for use; if a marked probe fails, the sender switches that media type to DSCP 0.

All packets from the SCTP association carrying data channels MUST use a single DSCP, which SHOULD be the one recommended for the highest-priority channel. All packets on one TCP connection MUST use a single DSCP.

A sender MUST support multiplexing all media and data on a single 5-tuple (fully bundled) and sending each media stream and data on its own 5-tuple (fully unbundled). Bundling by media type is optional. Sending data channel data over multiple 5-tuples is not supported. A receiver MUST be able to receive all these configurations.
sections.eli5: Packets can wear a colored sticker saying how urgent they are. If the network throws away stickered packets, the browser just stops using stickers.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: This document has no IANA actions. It adds no security text of its own: WebRTC security considerations are enumerated in RFC 8826, and those pertaining to DSCP use are in RFC 8837.
sections.eli5: The safety rules live in other documents, and this one has nothing new for the official lists.
